title: What a Soundscape Is: Three Layers, Never Blurred
description: A soundscape is everything audible in a place over a period of time, and soundscape ecology studies it as a whole while keeping its three layers distinct. Biophony is the sounds living organisms make: animal calls, songs, and choruses. Geophony is the sounds of the earth itself: wind, rain, thunder, running water, and waves. Anthrophony is the sounds humans make: traffic, machinery, aircraft, music, and voices. The layers are cross-linked, because animals must communicate through geophony and anthrophony, and because each layer shapes the others, but they are never blurred into one undifferentiated noise: every record in this pair states which layer or layers it covers, so a reader can always tell a bird from the wind behind it and from the road beyond that.

title: Biophony: The Living Layer
description: Biophony is the layer of sound produced by living organisms in an ecosystem: bird song at dawn, insect choruses at night, frog calls at a pond, whale song in the ocean, and the rustle and footfall of animals moving. Biophony varies by place, season, and time of day, and it carries ecological information: which species are present, whether they are breeding, and how healthy a habitat is. A rich biophony with many species calling in different frequency bands and time slots suggests a diverse community, while a silent habitat may signal disturbance, even when it looks intact. This record covers biophony alone, and it names the other layers only to keep them distinct: the wind behind the chorus is geophony, and any road noise is anthrophony.

title: Geophony: The Earth's Own Sounds
description: Geophony is the layer of sound produced by non-living natural processes: wind moving through trees, rain on leaves, thunder rolling across a plain, streams running over rock, waves breaking on a shore, and the deep groan of moving ice. Geophony shapes the other layers: animals evolved to call in frequency bands and at times when geophony is quieter, and a soundscape's geophony tells a listener about weather, terrain, and water even with eyes closed. Geophony is also the baseline against which change is measured: a stream that stops flowing changes a valley's soundscape before any animal leaves. This record covers geophony alone, kept distinct from the biophony of animals that live in the wind and rain and from the anthrophony of human machines.

title: Anthrophony: The Human-Made Layer
description: Anthrophony is the layer of sound humans make: road traffic, aircraft, construction machinery, sirens, music, and voices, including the low-frequency rumble of engines and the broadband roar of highways. Anthrophony is the youngest layer in evolutionary terms, and it is also the loudest in many modern soundscapes, masking animal calls, disrupting breeding choruses, and changing how animals use a habitat. Unlike geophony, anthrophony follows human schedules: rush hours, flight paths, and work shifts, so its pattern in a soundscape reveals human activity as clearly as biophony reveals animal activity. This record covers anthrophony alone, kept distinct from the biophony it masks and the geophony it overlays.

title: The Acoustic Niche Hypothesis
description: The acoustic niche hypothesis, proposed by Bernie Krause, states that in a healthy ecosystem, species evolve to vocalise in their own acoustic niches, distinct frequency bands and time slots, so that their calls do not mask each other, much as species divide food resources. A dawn chorus is the classic illustration: different birds sing at different pitches and in different minutes, insects occupy other bands at night, and frogs take yet other slots, so the whole community can be heard at once. When a habitat is degraded and species are lost, the acoustic niches empty and the soundscape thins, which is why soundscape recordings can reveal ecological damage. This record's primary layer is biophony, the community of callers dividing the acoustic space, while geophony and anthrophony are the competing sounds that niches must also avoid.

title: Habitat Soundscape Comparison: Forest, Grassland, and Wetland
description: Different habitats sound different, and comparing their soundscapes is a core soundscape-ecology method. A mature forest soundscape is layered: insects high, birds in the middle, mammals low, with wind in the canopy as geophony. A grassland soundscape is more open: wind dominates geophony, and bird and insect calls carry far. A wetland soundscape is dominated by water geophony and frog and bird biophony, often with the densest choruses of any habitat. The same three layers appear in all three habitats, but their balance differs, and that balance is itself ecological data: a forest whose canopy birds have vanished sounds different from an intact forest even before a surveyor arrives. This record covers all three layers, stated separately for each habitat, never blurred.

title: The Dawn Chorus: A Daily Soundscape Event
description: The dawn chorus is the burst of bird song that begins before sunrise and peaks in the first hours of daylight, when many species sing at once to defend territories and attract mates after the night. Singing at dawn is thought to help because sound carries well in the cool, still morning air, and because a male that sings vigorously after a night without food honestly advertises his condition. The chorus follows a sequence: different species start at different light levels, so the chorus builds species by species, and it fades as the day warms and feeding takes over. This record's primary layer is biophony, the birds themselves, while the still morning air is geophony at its quietest and any early traffic is anthrophony intruding on the chorus.

title: Urban Soundscapes: When Anthrophony Dominates
description: In cities, anthrophony dominates the soundscape: traffic, construction, aircraft, and sirens form a near-constant background, often loudest at low frequencies, and biophony must fit around it. Urban birds adapt in documented ways: they sing louder, higher, and at quieter times, such as at night or in the early morning before rush hour, and some species shift their song pitch above the traffic rumble. But adaptation has limits, and species that cannot adjust disappear from the noisiest areas, so the urban soundscape is both a record of human activity and a filter on wildlife. This record covers biophony and anthrophony together, kept distinct: the birds are biophony, the traffic is anthrophony, and the story is their interaction, with geophony, such as urban wind and rain, as the third layer in the background.

title: Freshwater Soundscapes: Ponds, Streams, and Rivers
description: Freshwater soundscapes combine rich biophony with strong geophony. Ponds host frog choruses and insect stridulation, streams add the continuous geophony of flowing water over rock, and rivers add depth, current, and seasonal flood sounds. Underwater, fish produce grunts, clicks, and drumming sounds, and aquatic insects add their own signals, so a hydrophone in a pond hears a different world from a microphone above it. Freshwater soundscapes are sensitive indicators: pollution, water extraction, and invasive species change them, and their recording is a growing tool in freshwater conservation. This record covers biophony and geophony, kept distinct: the animals are biophony, the water itself is geophony, and anthrophony such as nearby roads or pumps is named separately when present.

title: Marine Soundscapes: The Ocean's Three Layers
description: Marine soundscapes contain all three layers in a medium where sound travels far and fast. Biophony includes whale song, dolphin whistles, fish choruses, and the snapping of shrimp, which dominates many shallow reefs. Geophony includes waves, surf, rain on the sea surface, and underwater earthquakes. Anthrophony includes shipping, sonar, seismic surveys, and construction, and it is the layer of greatest concern in marine conservation, because it masks whale communication over large areas. Because water carries low frequencies over great distances, a single ship can raise background levels across a wide area, and marine protected areas are increasingly managed with sound in mind. This record covers all three layers, stated separately, never blurred.

title: Seasonal Change in Soundscapes
description: Soundscapes change with the seasons, and those changes are ecological data. Spring brings breeding choruses of birds and frogs, summer brings insect choruses at night, autumn brings migrating flocks and rutting calls, and winter quiets most biophony while geophony, wind, storms, and ice, takes over. Recording the same site through a full year produces a soundscape calendar, and shifts in that calendar, such as earlier spring choruses, are evidence of broader environmental change. This record's primary layers are biophony and geophony, kept distinct: the seasonal arrival and departure of callers is biophony, while the seasonal weather that frames them is geophony, and anthrophony such as seasonal tourism or farming is named separately when it appears.

title: Soundscape Indices in Practice
description: Soundscape indices such as the Acoustic Complexity Index, the Acoustic Diversity Index, and the Normalised Difference Soundscape Index compress a recording into numbers that can be compared across sites and years. The Normalised Difference Soundscape Index, or NDSI, compares biophony in the 2 to 8 kilohertz band, where many birds and insects call, with anthrophony in the 1 to 2 kilohertz band, where much human noise lies, giving a value from minus one, anthrophony-dominated, to plus one, biophony-dominated. Indices are powerful for large datasets, but they are summaries, not substitutes for listening: a high diversity score can come from a storm as easily as from a chorus. Good practice therefore pairs indices with listening checks and states which layers each index responds to.

title: Noise Pollution and Its Effects on Wildlife
description: Noise pollution is anthrophony at levels that harm wildlife: it masks communication, so mates cannot find each other and alarms go unheard; it raises stress hormones; it drives animals from otherwise suitable habitat; and it changes predator-prey dynamics, because prey that cannot hear predators are caught more often. The effects are documented across birds, frogs, whales, and fish, and they occur even when the noise causes no physical injury, because communication itself is the casualty. Mitigation follows from the diagnosis: quieter roads, speed limits, noise barriers, quiet zones around breeding sites, and quieter ships all reduce masking, and soundscape monitoring measures whether they worked. This record covers biophony as the affected layer and anthrophony as the cause, kept distinct, with geophony as the natural background.

title: Restoration Ecology: Soundscapes That Come Back
description: When a habitat is restored, its soundscape is one of the first signs of recovery, and sometimes the earliest: replanted forests gain insect and bird voices before the canopy closes, rewetted wetlands regain frog choruses, and protected reefs regain fish and shrimp sounds. Soundscape monitoring is therefore used to judge restoration success, comparing restored sites with intact reference sites and with unrestored controls. The return of biophony does not by itself prove full recovery, since a few loud generalist species can dominate a still-degraded site, so restoration studies pair soundscape data with species surveys. This record covers all three layers: the returning biophony, the geophony of the restored landscape, and the anthrophony that restoration seeks to reduce.

title: Quiet Parks and Cultural Soundscapes
description: Some places are valued precisely for their soundscapes: national parks with natural quiet, recognised by programmes such as the United States National Park Service's Natural Sounds Program, and cultural soundscapes such as historic town squares, markets, and sacred sites, where human sounds are part of the heritage. Natural quiet is now rare and is treated as a resource to protect, because it supports wildlife communication and human restoration alike, and quiet parks are monitored for anthrophony intrusion from aircraft and roads. Cultural soundscapes raise a different question: which human sounds belong, and which are intrusion, a judgement that belongs to the community that lives with the soundscape. This record covers all three layers, with the judgement about anthrophony stated as a community matter, not as a technical fact.
